title: Chapter IV
focus: obsession and the discovery of life

teacherSummary.text: Victor works tirelessly, masters chemistry, and discovers the cause of life. Gathering materials from charnel houses and dissecting rooms, he neglects family and health for nearly two years as he builds a being of gigantic stature.

vocabulary.definition: To put off till to-morrow, or from day to day
vocabulary.context: I wished, as it were, to procrastinate all that related to my feelings of affection until the great object, which swallowed up every habit of my nature, should be completed.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: A house where beasts are butchered for the market
vocabulary.context: The dissecting room and the slaughterhouse furnished many of my materials; and often did my human nature turn with loathing from my occupation, whilst, still urged on by an eagerness which perpetually increased, I brought my work near to a conclusion.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

context.history: Body-snatching to supply anatomy schools was a real scandal of the era. 'Natural philosophy' was the period term for science.

significance: Victor withholds the secret from Walton, warning 'how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge'—the novel's core moral caution.
discussionQuestions: Victor refuses to tell Walton how he created life. Why is this choice important?
Where does foreshadowing appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the sublime power of nature?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter IV,” how does Shelley show obsession and the discovery of life? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter IV develops the idea of obsession and the discovery of life. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of foreshadowing and tone / mood shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses foreshadowing in Chapter IV to complicate the reader's understanding of obsession and the discovery of life. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter IV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of obsession and the discovery of life responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter IV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of obsession and the discovery of life. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

satQuestions.passage: I see by your eagerness, and the wonder and hope which your eyes express, my friend, that you expect to be informed of the secret with which I am acquainted; that cannot be: listen patiently until the end of my story, and you will easily perceive why I am reserved upon that subject. I will not lead you on, unguarded and ardent as I then was, to your destruction and infallible misery. Learn from me, if not by my precepts, at least by my example, how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge, and how much happier that man is who believes his native town to be the world, than he who aspires to become greater than his nature will allow.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: Victor refuses to tell Walton how he created life. Why is this choice important? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include procrastinate, slaughterhouse, dissecting, dabbled, charnel. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “I wished, as it were, to procrastinate all that related to my feelings of affection until the great object, which swallowed up every habit of my nature, should be completed.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: To put off till to-morrow, or from day to day.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Body-snatching to supply anatomy schools was a real scandal of the era. 'Natural philosophy' was the period term for science. Now, why does this chapter matter? Victor withholds the secret from Walton, warning 'how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge'—the novel's core moral caution. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Foreshadowing, Tone / mood, Imagery.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot foreshadowing, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
